--- title: "Market" --- Tenure, home values, rents, affordability, and cost burden for the Richmond region, from the ACS 5-year estimates. Every trend compares three non-overlapping five-year windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. ## Ownership held near two-thirds as both tenures grew ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-ownership-1.png){#fig-ownership fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the homeownership rate in Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the pooled core, the pooled expansion ring, and the region across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. Rates barely change over time. The expansion ring is highest at about 85 percent, Chesterfield is near 77 percent, and Richmond city is lowest at about 43 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Across the 17-locality region, 67.0% of households own their home in the 2024 window, against 66.2% in the 2014 window. - Richmond city is the only core locality where renters outnumber owners: 58,914 renter households to 45,407 owner households, an ownership rate of 43.5%. - Chesterfield (76.7%) and the expansion ring (85.5%) are overwhelmingly owner markets; Henrico sits between them at 64.5%. - Renter households grew 14.2% across the region and owner households 18.5% between the 2014 and 2024 windows. ::: {#tbl-tenure .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Owner- and renter-occupied households, 2014 and 2024 ACS 5-year windows. Source: ACS Table B25003.

````` ::: ::: - Chesterfield added 19,482 owner households and 5,668 renter households, the largest owner gain of the three core localities. - Richmond city added 9,705 renter households (19.7%), against 9.0% in Henrico and 21.0% in Chesterfield. ## Home values and rents climbed in every core locality ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-value-1.png){#fig-value fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of real median home value, in 2024 dollars, in the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia, with a dot for each window joined by a line.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The Richmond MSA's median home value rose 24.1% after inflation, from $284,755 to $353,500 in 2024 dollars (64.5% before adjusting). - Among the core three, Richmond city's real median value rose 36.6%, Henrico's rose 24.8%, and Chesterfield's rose 25.7%. - The metro's 2024 median ($353,500) compares with $383,700 statewide. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-rent-1.png){#fig-rent fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of real median gross rent, in 2024 dollars, in the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia, with a dot for each window joined by a line.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The Richmond MSA's median gross rent rose 11.3% in real terms, from $1,299.88 to $1,447 a month (47.5% as published). - Richmond city's real median rent rose 15.9%, against rose 13.0% in Henrico and rose 11.1% in Chesterfield. - Gross rent includes utilities the renter pays, so it is not comparable to a quoted asking rent. ::: {#tbl-medians .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: - Smaller localities carry wider margins of error on both medians; the table suppresses low-reliability cells and marks medium ones. - The "real change" columns deflate the earlier window to 2024 dollars with the national CPI-U, so they measure change relative to national prices, not a local cost-of-living index. ## Price-to-income ratios show where buying is hardest ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-pti-1.png){#fig-pti fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the ratio of median home value to median household income in Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024.' width=100%} ::: ::: - In the Richmond MSA the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the 2024 window, against 3.6 times in the 2014 window. - Among the core three, the ratio is 5.5 in Richmond city, 4.0 in Henrico, and 3.6 in Chesterfield; statewide it is 4.1. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-pti-renter-1.png){#fig-pti-renter fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the ratio of median home value to median renter household income in Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. The ratio is higher than the all-household version in every geography and rises in the Richmond metro from about 5.9 to about 6.5.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Measured against renter households, the typical Richmond MSA home was worth 6.5 times the typical renter income in the 2024 window, against 5.9 times in the 2014 window. - Among the core three, the renter ratio is 7.3 in Richmond city, 6.0 in Henrico, and 5.9 in Chesterfield; statewide it is 6.4. - This is the more relevant gap for renters weighing a move to ownership, but it is still a ratio of two medians: it does not say how many renters could qualify for a loan. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-rent-share-1.png){#fig-rent-share fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of annual median gross rent as a share of median household income in Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Annual median rent equals 25.5% of Richmond city's median household income, 20.8% of Henrico's, and 19.2% of Chesterfield's. - The ratio compares two medians, not one household's rent and income: renters are on average lower-income than the all-household median, so a typical renter's burden is higher than this ratio implies. The renter-income version below corrects for that, and the cost-burden section follows. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-rent-share-renter-1.png){#fig-rent-share-renter fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of annual median gross rent as a share of median renter household income in Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the Richmond metro, and Virginia across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. The share is higher than the all-household version in every geography.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Annual median rent equals 34.2% of Richmond city's median renter income, 31.0% of Henrico's, and 31.4% of Chesterfield's. - Rent and renter income are both renter-side medians, so this ratio is the closest single-number match to the cost-burden shares below (rent is gross rent; burden counts each household's own income). ::: callout-note ## What these ratios do and don't measure Median home value is the owner's own estimate of what their home is worth, for *every* owner-occupied home, not just recent sales, so the price-to-income ratio understates what it costs to enter the market today. The ratios appear twice, against all-household income and against renter-household income (ACS Table B25119); the renter version is the better yardstick for renters weighing a move to ownership. Both ratios divide one median by another; they describe how local prices compare with local incomes, not what any particular household can afford. ::: ## Renter cost burden stayed near half while owner burden fell ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-burden-trend-1.png){#fig-burden-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Six small line charts of the share of households paying 30 percent or more of income on housing, by tenure, across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024, for the region, the pooled core, Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, and the expansion ring. The renter line stays near 50 percent in most panels; the owner line falls from roughly 26 percent to 20 percent in the region.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Across the region, 51.2% of renter households pay 30% or more of income on housing in the 2024 window, against 51.4% in the 2014 window — effectively unchanged. 25.7% pay half or more. - Owner burden fell: 20.0% of owners are cost-burdened now, down from 26.1%. - Richmond city has the highest owner burden of the core three (26.2%, down from 33.9%). - Renter burden is nearly identical across the core: 52.0% in Richmond city, 51.6% in Henrico, and 52.2% in Chesterfield — a region-wide condition, not a city one. - The Richmond MSA's 51.2% renter burden compares with 48.5% statewide and 54.5% in Hampton Roads. ::: {#tbl-burden .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Share of households paying 30% or more of income on housing, by tenure, 2014 and 2024 ACS 5-year windows. Shares are of households with a computed burden. Sources: ACS Tables B25070 (renters) and B25091 (owners).
Geography Renters 2014 Renters 2024 Change (pts) Owners 2014 Owners 2024 Change (pts)
Richmond region 51.4% 51.2% -0.2 26.1% 20.0% -6.0
Richmond core 51.6% 51.9% +0.4 27.0% 20.6% -6.4
Richmond city 56.0% 52.0% -3.9 33.9% 26.2% -7.7
Henrico 48.4% 51.6% +3.2 26.3% 18.8% -7.5
Chesterfield 48.7% 52.2% +3.5 24.8% 19.7% -5.1
Expansion ring 46.5% 42.6% -3.9 24.1% 16.5% -7.6
````` ::: ::: - Richmond city's renter burden moved from 56.0% to 52.0% (-3.9 points), while Henrico's moved +3.2 points and Chesterfield's +3.5 points. - The expansion ring's renter burden is the lowest of the six geographies at 42.6%, but its renter base is small (10,638 households). - Excluded from every share: 9,537 renter and 2,706 owner households in the region with no computed burden (zero or negative income, or no cash rent). ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-burden-locality-1.png){#fig-burden-locality fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal stacked bar chart of the share of renter households paying 30 percent or more of income on housing in 2024, by locality, split into households paying 30 to 49 percent and those paying 50 percent or more. Only localities with reliable estimates are shown. Chesterfield, Richmond city, Henrico, and Petersburg all sit near or just above half.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The 10 localities with reliable renter-burden estimates all fall between 43.1% and 56.3%. - 7 of the 17 localities are omitted because their renter-burden estimates are too imprecise to show; they are mostly small, rural localities with few renter households. ## Home-purchase lending peaked in 2021 and has settled lower ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-hmda-orig-1.png){#fig-hmda-orig fig-align='left' fig-alt='Two line charts of mortgage loans originated for a principal residence, 2018 to 2025, in Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield. In the all-purposes panel, originations roughly double from 2018 to 2020 and 2021 on refinancing, then fall by more than half by 2023. In the home-purchase panel, originations rise modestly to 2021 and fall about a third by 2023. Chesterfield has the most loans in each panel, Henrico is second, and Richmond city has the fewest.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Across the core three, lenders originated 17,262 home-purchase loans for principal residences in 2021, the peak, and 10,607 in 2023, the low since (-38.6%). In 2025 it was 10,877. - Counting all purposes, originations were 49,661 in 2021, against 17,172 in 2023 and 20,984 in 2025; the swing is mostly refinancing, not buying. - In 2025, Chesterfield had 5,157 home-purchase originations, Henrico 3,729, and Richmond city 1,991. - Median originated loan in the core: $275,000 in 2018 and $365,000 in 2025 for home purchase (nominal dollars). ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-hmda-race-1.png){#fig-hmda-race fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of the home-purchase mortgage denial rate in the Richmond core, 2018 to 2025, for four groups of applicants. Black applicants have the highest denial rate, roughly 11 to 18 percent. Hispanic or Latino applicants are next, Asian applicants lower, and non-Hispanic White applicants lowest at roughly 4 to 5 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Over 2022-2025, 16.1% of Black applicants' home-purchase applications were denied, against 4.5% for non-Hispanic White applicants, 10.6% for Hispanic or Latino applicants, and 9.0% for Asian applicants. - The overall home-purchase denial rate in the core was 8.3% in 2025 and 8.2% in 2018 — little changed. The all-purposes rate is higher (18.9% in 2025) because refinance and home-improvement applications are denied more often. - Denial rates by locality in 2025 are close: 7.5% in Richmond city, 8.4% in Henrico, and 8.6% in Chesterfield. ::: {#tbl-hmda-reasons .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Reasons given for denial, all denied principal-residence applications in the core three, 2022-2025. A denial can cite up to four reasons, so shares sum to more than 100%. Source: FFIEC/CFPB HMDA.
Stated reason Denials Share of denied applications
Debt-to-income ratio 8,356 36%
Credit history 7,671 33%
Credit application incomplete 3,507 15%
Collateral 2,999 13%
Other 2,950 13%
Unverifiable information 1,343 6%
Insufficient cash 799 3%
Employment history 527 2%
Mortgage insurance denied 10 0%
````` ::: ::: - Debt-to-income (35.8%) and credit history (32.9%) are the most-cited reasons, together far ahead of collateral or cash. ::: callout-note ## How to read the lending figures HMDA covers most mortgage lenders but not every loan, and the denial rate describes **applications that reached a credit decision** (originated, approved-but-not-accepted, or denied); withdrawn and incomplete applications are not counted. Denial rates compare applicant groups but do not control for income, credit, or loan terms, so a gap is a flag for further review, not evidence of discrimination on its own. Race and ethnicity follow the grouping built in `r/hmda.R`; "Incomplete/No Data" and "Other Minority" are not charted because they are heterogeneous or small. Figures cover principal residences with one to four units. ::: ## Eviction filings fell sharply in 2020 and have not fully returned ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-evict-monthly-1.png){#fig-evict-monthly fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of monthly eviction filings from 2016 to 2026 in Richmond city, Henrico, and Chesterfield. All three run at roughly 600 to 1,800 filings a month before 2020, collapse to near zero in 2020 and 2021, then recover to a level below the pre-2020 peak. Richmond city is highest throughout, Henrico second, Chesterfield lowest.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Across the core three, filings peaked at 37,548 in 2016, then fell to 7,575 in 2021 — 79.8% below the peak. - The monthly low was 162 filings, in December 2020. - In the latest 12 months (through September 2026), the core averaged 2,558 filings a month, 15% below the 2016-2019 monthly average of 3,011. - Richmond city accounts for the largest share of filings: 42.8% of the core total in 2025, with Henrico at 33.2% and Chesterfield at 24.0%. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](market_files/figure-html/fig-evict-pct-1.png){#fig-evict-pct fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of eviction filings as a percent of each month\'s historical average for the Richmond core, 2016 to 2026, with a reference line at 100 percent. The series hovers near 100 percent through 2019, drops to roughly 20 percent in 2020 and 2021, and recovers to roughly 80 to 90 percent in the most recent years.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Filings ran at 103% of the historical average in 2018 and 91% in 2019, already easing before the pandemic. - The core bottomed at 21% of average in 2021, then climbed to 87% in 2025. - Over the latest 12 months the core stands at 85% of average; Chesterfield is closest to its baseline (97%) and Richmond city furthest (81%). ::: {#tbl-evict .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Defaults made up 38.9% of core filings in 2025, against 45.7% in 2018. - 2026 is a partial year (9 months), so its totals are not comparable to full years; 22,814 filings so far. ::: callout-note ## What eviction filings do and don't measure A filing is a landlord's court request, not a completed eviction: many cases are dismissed, settled, or paid before judgment, and a household can be filed against more than once. Filings are a signal of housing instability, not a count of households displaced. The 2020-2021 collapse reflects pandemic-era eviction moratoria and rental assistance as much as underlying need, so read the recovery against the pre-2020 baseline, not as a measure of the renter burden shown above. Counts cover the three core localities only; the expansion ring is not included. ::: ::: callout-warning ## Small-geography reliability Renter-burden and median estimates for the expansion-ring localities and other small jurisdictions rest on small samples. Figures here use the pooled rows or the three core localities where possible; locality-level cells with a coefficient of variation above 30 are omitted (—) and medium-reliability cells are marked (*). ::: ::: callout-note ## How cost burden is measured A household is **cost-burdened** when it pays 30% or more of its income on housing and **severely cost-burdened** at 50% or more. For renters, housing cost is gross rent, which includes utilities; for owners it is selected monthly owner costs, which include mortgage payments, taxes, insurance, and utilities. Households with no or negative income are excluded. ::: ::: callout-tip ## What this page shows - **Tenure:** about two-thirds of households own (67.0%), a share that barely moved, but Richmond city is a majority-renter locality (43.5% own). - **Values and rents:** the Richmond MSA's median home value rose 24.1% and median rent rose 11.3% after inflation. - **Affordability:** the typical home was worth 4.1 times the typical household income in the metro (6.5 times the typical renter income), and median rent equalled 20.0% of household income (31.7% of renter income). - **Cost burden:** about half of renter households (51.2%) are cost-burdened and that has not eased, while owner burden fell to 20.0%. - **Mortgage lending:** core-three home-purchase originations for principal residences peaked at 17,262 in 2021 and were 10,877 in 2025; Black applicants were denied 16.1% of the time against 4.5% for White applicants. - **Evictions:** core-three filings fell 80% from the pre-2020 peak to the 2021 trough and now run at about 85% of the historical average. :::
